title: Case debrief: 'WTI looks 3 % too cheap — do we trade it?'
rubric: Translates the situation: the log spread is ≈ 0.09 vs a long-run average of ≈ 0.06, i.e. WTI is ≈ 3 % cheap relative to the cointegrating relation (the ECT is negative).
Uses the ECM: with α ≈ −0.115, about 11.5 % of the gap closes per day; half-life ≈ 6 business days — so the expected convergence of ≈ 1.5 % takes about a week, with noise.
Grounds the signal in the economics: the arbitrage (export / transport) that drives the convergence; asks why the gap opened (a WTI-specific event?) and whether the arbitrage is currently possible.
Lists the statistical risks: β and α are estimated; Engle-Granger has low power and assumes one stable relation; the half-life is an average, individual deviations can widen first.

Names regime risk explicitly: a structural change (logistics, regulation) can move the equilibrium itself — then the 'gap' is the new normal and the trade loses; stability should be checked on sub-periods (Case 4).
Makes the economics of the trade concrete: expected move vs transaction costs and carry, position size vs the spread's daily volatility, an exit rule if the spread keeps widening.
Keeps the claim honest: the model describes how gaps closed historically; it is not a guarantee or a backtested strategy.
